person.name: Grace_Hopper
person.summary: Grace Brewster Hopper was an American computer scientist, mathematician, and U.S. Navy rear admiral. A pioneer of computer programming, she helped develop the Harvard Mark I, devised the theory of machine‑independent programming languages, and led creation of early compilers including FLOW‑MATIC, which strongly influenced COBOL. She served for decades in the Navy, shaping standards for programming languages and computer systems.

events.title: Birth in New York City
events.description: Grace Brewster Murray (later Grace Hopper) was born in New York City to Walter Fletcher Murray and Mary Campbell Van Horne. She was the eldest of three children in a family of Scottish and Dutch descent, and her great‑grandfather Alexander Wilson Russell had been an admiral in the U.S. Navy.

events.date_note: Year of graduation from Vassar College
events.title: Graduates from Vassar
events.description: Grace Murray completed her undergraduate studies at Vassar College, graduating Phi Beta Kappa with a bachelor’s degree in mathematics and physics. Her strong performance in mathematics set the foundation for her later work in mathematical physics and computer science.

events.title: Earns Yale master’s degree
events.description: Grace Murray received a master’s degree in mathematics from Yale University, further specializing in advanced mathematical theory. This achievement marked her transition from undergraduate work at Vassar to graduate‑level research at one of the leading American universities.

events.title: Marries Vincent Foster Hopper
events.description: Grace Murray married Vincent Foster Hopper, a professor at New York University. Although the couple later divorced in 1945, she continued to use the surname Hopper for the rest of her life and under that name became widely known as a pioneer in computing.

events.title: Joins Vassar mathematics faculty
events.description: Grace Hopper began teaching mathematics at Vassar College as an instructor. Over the next decade she developed her skills as a teacher and researcher, and in 1941 she was promoted to associate professor of mathematics, balancing academic responsibilities with her continuing graduate work.

events.title: Completes Yale Ph.D.
events.description: Grace Hopper earned her Ph.D. in mathematics from Yale University under the supervision of Øystein Ore. Her dissertation, titled "New Types of Irreducibility Criteria," was published in 1934, establishing her as a professional mathematician with expertise in abstract algebra.

events.title: Sworn into Navy Reserve
events.description: During World War II, Grace Hopper obtained a leave of absence from Vassar College and was sworn into the United States Navy Reserve as part of the WAVES program. Because she was below the minimum Navy weight requirement, she had to obtain a special exemption to receive her commission.

events.date_note: Assigned after graduating from Naval Reserve Midshipmen’s School in 1944; remained until 1949
events.title: Programs Harvard Mark I
events.description: After graduating first in her class at the Naval Reserve Midshipmen’s School, Lieutenant (junior grade) Grace Hopper was assigned to the Bureau of Ships Computation Project at Harvard University. There she served on the programming staff for the Harvard Mark I (Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator) under Howard H. Aiken, co‑authoring several papers and helping to write the machine’s first operational manual.

images.caption: Duty officer assignment sheet for the U.S. Navy Bureau of Ships Computation Project operating the Harvard Mark I at Harvard University.

events.date_note: Commonly mis‑dated as 1945; Smithsonian and other sources give 1947, but event is associated with Hopper’s Mark II work in the mid‑1940s
events.title: Documents famous computer bug
events.description: While working with the Harvard Mark II Aiken Relay Calculator, Grace Hopper’s team found a moth trapped in a relay—an incident they humorously logged as the "first actual case of bug being found." The taped moth and log entry became an iconic artifact in computing history and popularized the use of the term "debugging" for fixing computer problems.

images.caption: Logbook page from the Harvard Mark II showing the moth taped in place and labeled as the first actual computer "bug."

events.title: Joins Eckert–Mauchly for UNIVAC
events.description: Grace Hopper left Harvard in 1949 to become a senior mathematician at the Eckert–Mauchly Computer Corporation in Philadelphia, joining the team developing the UNIVAC I. She later became UNIVAC director of Automatic Programming Development for Remington Rand, working on some of the earliest commercial electronic computers.

images.caption: Grace Hopper at the UNIVAC keyboard around 1960, working with one of the first commercial electronic computers.

events.title: Builds first A-0 compiler
events.description: While working for Remington Rand, Grace Hopper completed an operational link‑loader for the A‑0 System, which she described as a compiler. Her A‑0 compiler translated symbolic mathematical notation into machine code and demonstrated that computers could be programmed using higher‑level representations rather than only numeric codes, laying groundwork for modern programming languages.

location_coordinates.name: Philadelphia

events.title: Leads automatic programming department
events.description: Grace Hopper was appointed the first director of automatic programming at Remington Rand. Under her leadership, the department released early compiler‑based programming languages such as MATH‑MATIC and FLOW‑MATIC, pioneering the idea that business data processors could write programs using English‑like statements instead of low‑level symbolic codes.

events.date_note: The CODASYL conference that initiated COBOL took place in the spring of 1959; exact start day varies by source
events.title: Advises CODASYL on COBOL
events.description: In the spring of 1959, Grace Hopper served as a technical consultant to the Conference on Data Systems Languages (CODASYL), which brought together government and industry experts to design a new business programming language. Drawing heavily on her FLOW‑MATIC work, the committee created COBOL, a machine‑independent, English‑like language that would become the dominant language for business data processing.

location_coordinates.name: Washington, D.C.

events.title: Heads Navy Programming Languages Group
events.description: Recalled to active duty in 1967, Grace Hopper became director of the Navy Programming Languages Group in the Office of Information Systems Planning. Over the next decade she oversaw development of validation software and led COBOL standardization efforts across the Navy, helping to unify programming practices and ensure compatibility among systems. She was promoted to captain in 1973.

images.caption: Insignia representing the rank of captain in the United States Navy, which Hopper achieved while directing the Navy Programming Languages Group.

events.title: Promoted to commodore at White House
events.description: On December 15, 1983, Grace Hopper was promoted on the retired list to the U.S. Navy rank of commodore (later redesignated rear admiral, lower half). The ceremony took place at the White House, where Secretary of the Navy John Lehman officiated and President Ronald Reagan attended, recognizing Hopper’s decades of service and pioneering contributions to computer technology.

images.caption: Grace Hopper being promoted to the rank of commodore at the White House, with Secretary of the Navy John Lehman and President Ronald Reagan.

location_coordinates.label: Washington, District of Columbia, United States
location_coordinates.name: Washington, D.C.

events.title: Retires from U.S. Navy
events.description: Grace Hopper retired from the United States Navy on August 14, 1986, after more than 42 years of combined active and reserve service. At the time of her retirement as a rear admiral (lower half), she was the oldest serving officer in the Navy and received the Defense Distinguished Service Medal in recognition of her extraordinary contributions to military computing and information systems.

images.caption: Ribbon for the Defense Distinguished Service Medal, awarded to Grace Hopper upon her retirement from the Navy.

events.title: Death in Arlington, Virginia
events.description: Grace Hopper died on January 1, 1992, in Arlington, Virginia. Her death marked the end of a career that had reshaped both military and commercial computing through her work on early computers, compilers, and programming language standards.
